title: Why the Brain’s Right Hemisphere Controls Your Left Side: Expert Q&A Explained
body:
The brain’s left‑right wiring has long puzzled scientists, but a recent interview with Dr. Martin Wessendorf, an emeritus associate professor of neuroscience at the University of Minnesota, sheds new light on why the right hemisphere governs the left side of the body. Drawing on decades of research into brainstem‑spinal connections, Wessendorf explains that the asymmetrical control pattern is rooted in evolutionary development, neural circuitry efficiency and the way motor commands are routed through the spinal cord. His insights not only clarify a fundamental aspect of human neuroanatomy but also open avenues for treating spinal injuries and neurodegenerative diseases.

At the core of the explanation is the brainstem, the ancient structure that links the cerebral cortex with the spinal cord. Wessendorf’s work has demonstrated that the brainstem houses a series of descending pathways—most notably the corticospinal tract—that cross over, or decussate, at the level of the medulla oblongata. This crossing causes motor signals originating in the right motor cortex to descend on the left side of the spinal cord, ultimately innervating muscles on the left side of the body. “The decussation is not an accident,” Wessendorf notes. “It is a highly conserved feature across vertebrates, suggesting a functional advantage that has been selected for over millions of years.”

One hypothesis for that advantage relates to sensorimotor integration. When an organism moves, sensory feedback from the limbs travels back to the brain through the dorsal columns, which also cross to the opposite side of the brainstem. By having both motor output and sensory input converge on the same cortical hemisphere, the brain can process and adjust movements more rapidly. This bilateral crossing thus streamlines the loop between perception and action, reducing latency in reflexes and coordinated motions. The arrangement also allows for redundancy; if one side of the brain suffers damage, the opposite side can sometimes compensate, preserving basic motor function.

Wessendorf’s research further highlights the role of spinal interneurons that receive these crossed signals. In animal models, he has mapped how specific brainstem nuclei modulate spinal circuits responsible for posture, locomotion and fine motor control. The findings suggest that the brainstem does more than simply relay commands; it fine‑tunes them based on ongoing sensory input, effectively acting as a real‑time processor that tailors motor output to the body’s current state. This nuanced view challenges older models that portrayed the brainstem as a passive conduit and underscores its importance in both health and disease.

The implications of understanding this cross‑wiring extend to clinical practice. For patients with unilateral brain injuries—such as stroke or traumatic brain injury—the knowledge that motor pathways are contralateral informs rehabilitation strategies that aim to harness neuroplasticity in the unaffected hemisphere. Moreover, spinal cord injuries that disrupt the crossed tracts could be addressed through targeted neuromodulation or stem‑cell therapies designed to restore or bypass the decussated pathways. “If we can map precisely how the brainstem orchestrates these signals, we can develop interventions that mimic or augment its function,” Wessendorf says.

Looking ahead, the next frontier involves integrating high‑resolution imaging, electrophysiology and computational modeling to create a comprehensive atlas of brainstem‑spinal communication. Such an atlas could reveal subtle variations in decussation patterns among individuals, potentially explaining why some people recover more fully from neurological insults than others. As research progresses, the age‑old question of why the right brain controls the left side of the body moves from a curiosity to a cornerstone of translational neuroscience, promising new therapies that could one day restore movement to those who have lost it.
